warmup.q: The card reader's program needs 10 ms (milliseconds) of work for each payment. On a quiet morning it's busy half the time, and a payment takes 20 ms on average, counting any wait in line. At lunchtime more people pay, and it's busy 90% of the time. Each payment still needs 10 ms of work. Roughly how long does a payment take on average now?
options: About 22 ms, because the work per payment hasn't changed
About 36 ms: 1.8 times the payments, so 1.8 times the time
warmup.why: Each payment still needs 10 ms of work, but now it usually finds others in line ahead of it. For one worker with payments arriving at random, the average time is the work divided by (1 minus the share of time the worker is busy): 10 / 0.5 = 20 ms on a quiet morning, and 10 / 0.1 = 100 ms at lunchtime. The first section builds this rule up. Waiting grows much faster than the number of payments, which is why the first two answers are too low. A full second is where it goes at 99% busy.

sections.h: Where a payment's time goes: work, waiting and a busy worker
sections.html:
Let's time one payment. When you tap your card, the café's payment program sends a request to your bank, a message that asks "may this card pay 3.50?", and waits for the answer. The program's own clock says the round trip took 120 ms (milliseconds). The bank's records say it spent 20 ms on the request. Both are right, because they measured different things.

The response time is what the waiting side sees: from sending the request until the answer is back. The service time is the part when something is actively working on the request, the bank's 20 ms. The other 100 ms went on waiting. Part of it was travel over the network, the cables and radio links between computers, and part was sitting in a line before anyone picked the request up, which is called queueing. In this course, latency means that waiting: the time a request is latent, lying still while nobody works on it. Many people mix up latency and response time, so keep them apart.

A shop with one till shows where waiting comes from. The cashier takes about a minute per customer, and customers walk in at random. Sometimes two arrive together, and one of them waits. In programming terms, the cashier is a worker, a part of the program that handles one request at a time. Each customer is a request, and the line is a queue. A computer has many such lines, and you can't see any of them. A request may wait for a free connection (an open line to the bank's computer), for a free worker, and at the disk that stores the data.

How long the line gets depends on how busy the worker is. Utilization is the share of time a worker is busy: requests per second times the service time of each. Fifty requests a second at 10 ms each gives 0.5, busy half the time. When requests arrive at random and need a random amount of work, the textbook model gives one worker's average, or mean, response time:

mean response time = service time / (1 - utilization)

With 10 ms of work, that's 20 ms at 50% busy, 50 ms at 80% and 100 ms at 90%. At 95% it's 200 ms, and at 99% a full second. Nothing about the requests changed. Each one found more requests ahead of it. The figure draws that curve. It's why a program that looks fine at 70% busy falls over at 95%. If every request took exactly 10 ms, the waiting would halve, but the curve would bend the same way.

Waiting grows much faster than load. Keep spare room.

One more rule ties waiting to sizes. Little's law says that, in any system that keeps up with its work, the average number of requests inside equals the arrival rate times the average time each one spends inside. Written short, it's L = λ × W: L is the number inside, λ (the Greek letter lambda) is the arrival rate, and W is the time each one spends. It holds however the times are spread. At 2,000 payments a second and 50 ms each, 100 payments are in progress at any moment. Now say the program keeps only 20 open connections to the bank and reuses them. Then 80 payments wait for a free connection before they even leave the program. That wait counts in the response time, and the bank never sees it.

So far we've talked about averages. Next, we'll see what an average hides.

figure.caption: One worker, 10 ms of work per request. The work never changes; the waiting does. At 90% busy the mean response time is 100 ms.

try.title: Push a queue towards 100% busy
steps: From the labs folder, run the demo below. It pretends to be one worker on a simulated clock, so it finishes in a moment. Each row sends a million requests that arrive at random, each needing a random amount of work that averages 10 ms.
Before you run it, predict the mean and the p99 at 95% busy. (The p99 is the time that 99 of every 100 requests stay within; the next section explains it.)
Compare the last two columns. One counts the requests inside the system at random moments, and the other multiplies the arrival rate by the mean time. Why should they agree?

code.title: QueueDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: for (i in 0 until n) { t += exp(rnd, meanGap) // the next arrival, at random val service = exp(rnd, MEAN_SERVICE_MS) // random work, mean 10 ms val start = maxOf(t, freeAt) // wait in line if the worker is busy freeAt = start + service arrive[i] = t depart[i] = freeAt }

try.expect:
one worker, mean service time 10 ms, 1,000,000 requests per row
busy   formula S/(1-p)   measured mean   measured p99   in system   rate x mean
 50%           20 ms           20 ms           92 ms         1.0           1.0
 80%           50 ms           50 ms          231 ms         4.0           4.0
 90%          100 ms           99 ms          442 ms         9.1           8.9
 95%          200 ms          196 ms          924 ms        18.9          18.6
 99%         1000 ms          903 ms         3880 ms        89.3          89.4
90% busy, every request exactly 10 ms: mean 54 ms, p99 215 ms

In the header, S/(1-p) is the rule above, with S for the service time and p for utilization. The measured means follow the rule. The 99% row comes out a little low: at 99% busy the line swings so widely that a million requests aren't enough to average it out. The p99 is about 4.6 times the mean in every row, and it climbs as steeply. The last two columns check Little's law. Counting the requests inside the system at 10,000 random moments gives the same number as the arrival rate times the mean time. The simulation starts from a fixed seed (the number that decides which random values come out), so you get exactly these numbers.

sections.h: Why the average hides the slow payments: percentiles
sections.html:
Here are ten response times from the card reader's program, in milliseconds, sorted from fastest to slowest:

12  13  13  14  15  15  16  18  22  940

The mean is 107.8 ms, the number the café owner saw. No payment took anywhere near that. Nine took 22 ms or less, and one took almost a second. The mean blends the two groups into a number that describes neither.

Read positions off the sorted list instead. The median is the middle value: half the requests were faster and half slower. Here it's 15 ms, what a typical customer waits. It's also called p50, the 50th percentile. In general, a percentile is the time that a given share of requests stayed within. The p99 is the value that 99% of requests were at or below, and the p99.9 (sometimes written p999) is the same for 99.9%. These high percentiles describe the tail, the slow end. (Ten values can't give you a p99; you need thousands.)

Why care about one request in a hundred? Because the people who hit it are often the ones who matter most. The slowest requests tend to belong to the customers with the most data, such as the shop with the most payments to add up. Amazon set its internal speed targets at the p99.9 for that reason, as its 2007 paper on Dynamo, a database it built for its online shop, explains. And when one screen needs many requests, most screens hit the tail, as the fourth section works out.

Percentiles have one trap: you can't average them. Big companies run several copies of one program on separate computers to share the work, and the demo's output calls each copy a pod. Say ten copies share the payments equally. Nine have a p99 of 25 ms. The tenth shares its computer with another busy program, and 15% of its requests take 900 ms, so its p99 is 900 ms. The average of the ten p99s is 113 ms. The true p99 of all payments is 900 ms. That copy's slow requests are 1.5% of all requests, and a p99 sets aside only the slowest 1%, so it lands among them.

So keep counts, not percentiles. A histogram splits the possible times into ranges, called buckets, and counts how many requests fell into each. Counts add up. Add the ten copies' histograms bucket by bucket, and you have the histogram of all payments. From it you can read any percentile.

Good buckets are narrow for small values and wide for large ones. Make each bucket about 2% wider than the one before, which is called logarithmic buckets. Then every value the histogram reports is within 1% of a value really recorded. About 1,100 such buckets cover everything from a microsecond (a millionth of a second) to an hour. HdrHistogram, by Gil Tene, and DDSketch, from the monitoring company Datadog, are free libraries (ready-made code that other programs can use) built on this idea. The lab builds a small one.

Never average percentiles. Add the counts, then read the percentile.

A histogram is only as honest as the times we put into it, though. Next, we'll see how the usual way of testing speed records the wrong times.

try.title: Average ten p99s, then do it properly
steps: Run the demo below from the labs folder. Ten copies of the program (the pods) get 10,000 requests each, and pod 9 is slow for 15% of its requests.
Before the last three lines print, write down your guess for the true p99 of all 100,000 requests.
Change 15 to 9 in PercentileDemo.kt and run it again. Which of the two p99 lines moves?

code.title: PercentileDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: val averagedP99 = pods.map { quantile(it, 0.99) }.average() val all = pods.flatMap { it.asList() }.toLongArray().also { it.sort() } // what merging histograms gives you println("average of the ten p99s: %.0f ms".format(averagedP99)) println("p99 of all %,d requests: %d ms".format(all.size, quantile(all, 0.99)))

pod   requests   mean    p50    p99

average of the ten p99s:  113 ms
p99 of all 100,000 requests: 900 ms
service mean 32 ms, p50 19 ms, p90 24 ms, p99.9 900 ms

(output trimmed). Pod 9's p50 is 20 ms, like the others: most of its requests are fine. Its slow 15% are 1.5% of all traffic, more than the 1% a p99 leaves out. So the true p99 is 900 ms, while the averaged figure says 113 ms. With 9% instead of 15%, the slow requests would be 0.9% of the traffic. The true p99 would drop to about 25 ms, and the average of p99s would still say 113 ms, now wrong in the other direction. Look at the mean too, 32 ms: it hides the problem completely.

aside.title: Why not report the slowest request instead?
aside.html: The maximum is one request, and one request can be a fluke: a computer that paused once, or a hiccup on the network. It also only grows as you collect more times, so two days of different lengths can't be compared fairly. A p99 or p99.9 rests on many requests, so it moves when something real changes. Still, keep an eye on the maximum next to the percentiles. The next section shows a case where the maximum is the only number telling the truth.

sections.h: A speed test that lies: coordinated omission
sections.html:
Before a busy holiday, you want to know how the payments program copes with 1,000 payments a second. So you run a load test: a second program that pretends to be lots of card readers and times every answer. The usual tool works like this. It opens 10 connections to the program. On each one it sends a request, waits for the answer, writes down how long it took, then sends the next. Each connection is paced at 100 requests a second, 1,000 in all. The report says p99 = 6.23 ms.

Now freeze the program for 1.4 seconds in the middle of the run, and test again. A long garbage collection can do that: Java and Kotlin programs stop now and then to clear away memory they no longer use. The report barely changes: p99 = 9.02 ms. Only the maximum, 1.40 s, gives the pause away. Real customers don't wait for each other. At 1,000 a second, 1,400 of them would have tapped a card during the pause, and each would have waited up to 1.4 seconds.

What went wrong? The tester stopped sending while the program was stuck. Each of its 10 connections had one request out, waited 1.4 s for it, and recorded one slow time. The 1,400 requests it should have sent during the pause went out late, after the program woke up. Each was timed from when it finally left, so each looked fast. The stepper below shows it, one moment at a time. In effect, the tester agreed with the program not to measure during the bad moment. Gil Tene, the author of HdrHistogram, named this coordinated omission.

A tester that waits for each answer before sending the next request follows a closed model. One that sends at a fixed rate, whatever the program is doing, follows an open model, and that's how customers behave.

There are two fixes. Use an open model, and time every request from when it was planned to go out, as wrk2, another free tester, does with its -R option. Or keep the closed loop, but time each request from its planned send time instead of its actual one, which wrk2 calls correction. In this lesson's simulation, both give p99 = 1.28 s. The wrk2 instructions show the same on a real server, a computer that answers requests: with a 1.4 s pause, the corrected p99 is 1.27 s and the uncorrected one is 6.04 ms, about 200 times smaller.

Time a request from when it should have left. Send on schedule.

The same trap waits in a test you might write yourself, with 50 threads (paths of work that run at the same time) each looping send, wait and time. It measures how fast the program works, not how long customers wait. One habit catches all of these: read the maximum next to the p99. A maximum far above a calm p99 is the fingerprint of coordinated omission.

Even an honest test times one request at a time, though. Next, we'll see what happens when one screen needs a hundred answers.

try.title: Run the lying load test
steps: Run the demo below from the labs folder. It runs three testers against a simulated program: first a quiet one, then one that freezes for 1.4 s at t = 10 s (ten seconds into the run).
Predict the closed model's p99 with the freeze before you look.
Find the one column where the closed run, timed from the actual send, admits that something happened.

code.title: LyingLoadTestDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: // closed: send, wait for the answer, then send the next (late if the answer was late) val done = server.submit(sendAt) actual += done - sendAt // timed from the actual send planned += done - plannedAt // timed from when it should have been sent ready += Triple(maxOf(plannedAt + interval, done), plannedAt + interval, c) // open: request i goes out at i / rate, whatever the server is doing LongArray(30_000) { i -> (i * 1_000_000L / RATE).let { server.submit(it) - it } }

try.expect:
-- quiet server
                               count        p50        p90        p99      p99.9        max
closed, timed from send        30000    0.51 ms    3.16 ms    6.23 ms    8.50 ms   10.82 ms
closed, timed from plan        30000    0.51 ms    3.16 ms    6.23 ms    8.50 ms   10.82 ms
open, fixed arrival rate       30000    0.51 ms    3.16 ms    6.23 ms    8.50 ms   10.82 ms
-- server frozen for 1.4 s at t=10 s
                               count        p50        p90        p99      p99.9        max
closed, timed from send        30000    0.54 ms    4.58 ms    9.02 ms   12.79 ms     1.40 s
closed, timed from plan        30000    0.54 ms     0.18 s     1.28 s     1.39 s     1.40 s
open, fixed arrival rate       30000    0.54 ms     0.18 s     1.28 s     1.39 s     1.40 s

With a quiet program, all three agree. With the pause, the closed run timed from the actual send hides it everywhere except the maximum. Timed from the plan, the same closed run matches the open one. The p90 of 0.18 s is the backlog: after the pause, the one worker needs a while to catch up with 1,400 waiting requests while new ones keep arriving. The run uses a simulated clock, so it takes a fraction of a second and always prints these numbers.

sections.h: When one screen waits for a hundred answers: fan-out and the tail
sections.html:
The café owner opens the app's home screen. To draw it, the program asks 100 other places for a piece each, all at the same moment, and waits until every answer is back. Those places might be 100 small programs, or 100 shards, pieces of one big database split across computers. Call each one a leaf. A leaf is quick, 5 to 15 ms, except one time in a hundred, when it hits a pause and takes a full second. What does the owner see?

The screen is slow if any one leaf is slow. The chance that all 100 are fast is 0.99 multiplied by itself 100 times, written 0.99^100, which is 0.366. So 63% of screens take a second or more. A slowdown that touched 1% of one leaf's answers now touches most people. When one request causes many requests behind it, that's called fan-out. This effect is called tail latency amplification: fan-out turns the rare slow tail into the normal case.

Jeff Dean and Luiz André Barroso of Google described it in "The Tail at Scale" (2013), with the same sums. A server that usually answers in 10 ms, but takes a second at its p99, makes 63% of requests slow at a fan-out of 100. Even with one slow answer in 10,000, a fan-out of 2,000 makes almost one request in five slower than a second. In a real Google service they measured, one leaf answered within 10 ms at the p99, but waiting for all the leaves took 140 ms at the p99.

So a leaf needs a far stricter target than the screen. To keep only 1% of screens slow at a fan-out of 100, each leaf may be slow only 0.01% of the time.

You can't make every leaf perfect, but you can stop waiting for the unlucky one. A hedged request sends a second copy of a slow request to a replica, another computer that holds a copy of the same data, and takes whichever answer comes first. Send the hedge only once a request has been out longer than the leaf's p95 (the time 95% of its answers beat). Then it adds only about 5% more requests. The paper tested it on BigTable, a database Google built for huge tables, reading 1,000 values spread over 100 servers. Hedging after 10 ms cut the p99.9 from 1,800 ms to 74 ms, and sent only 2% more requests. A tied request goes further. It puts the request in line on two servers at once, each told about the other, and whichever starts first cancels its twin.

Hedging works only under two conditions. First, slowness must strike replicas separately. If the cause is shared, such as the same faulty new version of the program on every replica, or one overloaded disk under all of them, the hedge is slow too. Second, the request must be safe to run twice, which is called idempotent. Reading a balance is. A card payment is only if it carries an idempotency key, a unique label the bank checks so that a repeated request is charged once.

Next, we'll decide how slow is too slow, and write that down as a promise.

try.title: Fan out, then hedge
steps: Run the demo below from the labs folder. Each simulated screen fans out to N leaves. A leaf takes 5 to 15 ms, or a full second one time in 100.
Predict the share of slow screens at 100 leaves before it prints.
Predict what hedging after 15 ms does to the p99 and the p99.9, and how many extra requests it costs. Then look at the last row: why does hedging stop working there?

code.title: FanOutDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: val latency = if (hedgeAfter == null || first <= hedgeAfter) first else { hedges++; minOf(first, hedgeAfter + second) } // first answer wins slowest = maxOf(slowest, latency) // the page waits for all leaves

try.expect:
leaves   slow requests   formula 1 - 0.99^N
     1            1.1%                 1.0%
    10            9.5%                 9.6%
   100           63.2%                63.4%
  1000          100.0%               100.0%

100 leaves                     p50       p99     p99.9   extra requests
no hedging                  1000 ms    1000 ms    1000 ms        0.0%
hedge after 15 ms             23 ms      30 ms    1000 ms        1.0%
hedge, slowness shared      1000 ms    1000 ms    1000 ms        1.0%

With 100 leaves, even the median screen takes a second. Hedging after 15 ms (later than any fast leaf) sends 1% more requests and brings the p99 down to 30 ms. The p99.9 stays at a second: one leaf request in 10,000 has both copies slow, and with 100 leaves that happens on 1% of screens. When the slowness is shared, the hedge is as slow as the first try, and the same 1% of extra requests buys nothing.

sections.h: Turning the slow end into a promise: targets and error budgets
sections.html:
A train company doesn't promise that every train will be on time. It promises that, say, 99 trains in 100 arrive within 5 minutes of the timetable, counted each month. A p99 is the same kind of number, and it helps only once you've decided what it should be. To keep a promise like that, the company needs a measurement, a target, and a plan for the trains that will be late. Google's books on keeping large systems running, called Site Reliability Engineering (SRE), gave these the names most teams use.

A service level indicator (SLI) is the measurement, defined exactly. For the payments program, it might be "the share of card payments that get an answer, not an error, within 300 ms, measured at the load balancer." A load balancer is the machine at the front door that hands each request to one of the copies of the program. Where you measure is part of the definition. At the front door you see the time spent in lines and on the network; inside one copy, you don't.

A service level objective (SLO) is the target for that measurement over a stretch of time, called the window: "99.9% of card payments are good, over 30 days." An SLA (service level agreement) is an SLO written into a contract, with a price for missing it, such as money back. If nothing happens when you miss it, it's an SLO.

The 0.1% that may go wrong is the error budget. Over 30 days, 99.9% allows 43.2 minutes of complete outage (time when nothing works), or 0.1% of requests failing all month, or any mix of the two. 99.99% allows 4.32 minutes, and 99.999% about 26 seconds. The budget turns arguments into arithmetic. If little of it is used, the team can release the risky change. If it's nearly gone, they slow down and fix things first, like the train company spending its late trains on track repairs.

Last, decide when to wake a person up. Teams call that kind of alert a page. The burn rate compares how fast the budget is being spent with the steady pace that would spend exactly all of it by the end of the window. A burn rate of 1 uses the whole budget in 30 days. The SRE Workbook recommends a page when the burn rate over the last hour is 14.4, which means that hour alone used 2% of the month's budget. It also pages at a burn rate of 6 over the last 6 hours (5%). At 1 over 3 days (10%) it opens a ticket, a note to deal with in working hours. Each alert also checks a short window, 5 minutes for the one-hour alert, so it stops soon after the problem does. A total outage burns at 1,000 and empties a 99.9% budget in about 43 minutes. Paging on every burst of errors instead can wake someone up to 144 times a day while the promise is still being kept.

Promise a percentile over a window, and spend the budget on purpose.

A promise says how often the program may fail. It doesn't say why things fail, and that's the next lesson.

try.title: Spend an error budget by hand
steps: The payments program promises 99.95% good requests over 30 days, and it handles a steady 1,200 requests a second.
1. How many failed requests does the month's budget allow?
1. A bad update makes 3% of requests fail for 20 minutes, and then the team puts the old version back. What burn rate is that, and how much of the budget did it use?
1. Would the one-hour alert (burn rate 14.4 over the last hour, and over the last 5 minutes) have fired before the old version was back? When?
try.expect:
1. 30 days is 2,592,000 seconds, so the program handles 1,200 × 2,592,000 = 3,110,400,000 requests. 0.05% of that is 1,555,200 failed requests. As time, a total outage would use it up in 21.6 minutes.
  2. 3% failing against a 0.05% allowance is a burn rate of 60. In 20 minutes the program handled 1,440,000 requests, and 3% of them, 43,200, failed: 2.8% of the month's budget.
  3. Over the one-hour window, the burn rate climbs by 1 for every minute of the incident (60 × minutes ÷ 60), so it passes 14.4 after about 14.4 minutes. The 5-minute window is far above 14.4 by then. The alert fires about 14 minutes in, before the old version is back at 20 minutes. The 6-hour rule needs 36 minutes at this rate, so it never fires.

If your answer to question 2 came out in minutes, divide by the window: 20 minutes at a burn rate of 60 is 1,200 minutes at the steady pace, out of 43,200 minutes in 30 days. That's the same 2.8%.

Google SRE Workbook: Alerting on SLOs

opening:
Picture a busy Saturday at the café. Each customer taps a card, and the reader beeps almost at once. Then, every so often, it sits there for nearly a second before it beeps, and the person behind sighs. The owner checks the app: a payment takes about 108 milliseconds (thousandths of a second) on average.

The average is a real number, and so is the long pause. The trap is to trust the average because it's one tidy number, the one every report shows first. It mixes the quick payments and the slow ones into one value.

The first lesson, What a data system is, built the program behind that card reader, and ended on a question: how fast is it, and for whom? In this lesson, we'll split a payment's time into work and waiting, and see why waiting explodes when the program gets busy. We'll swap the average for better numbers, catch a test that hides slow moments, and turn the slow end into a promise. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at the café, with a card reader that usually beeps at once and sometimes takes a second, and an average that hid it. The slow moments were real. Percentiles show them, honest tests catch them, and a target with a budget says how many we can afford.

Try this on any website. Open your browser's developer tools (F12 on most computers, Command-Option-I on a Mac), choose the Network tab and reload the page. Each row is one request, with its time. Sort by time and look at the slowest few.

Next, we'll look at the parts that break, and ask how a system keeps its promise when a disk dies or a bug ships.

compare.title: A closed load loop and an open one

a.label: Closed model
a.title: waits for each answer
a.html: // one connection sends, waits, records, then sends the next fun closedLoop(client: Client, ratePerSecond: Int, durationNanos: Long, histogram: LogHistogram) { val interval = 1_000_000_000L / ratePerSecond val end = System.nanoTime() + durationNanos var slot = System.nanoTime() while (slot < end) { LockSupport.parkNanos(slot - System.nanoTime()) // wait for the slot (no wait if late) val sentAt = System.nanoTime() client.authorize() // blocks while the server is stuck histogram.record((System.nanoTime() - sentAt) / 1_000) // µs from the ACTUAL send slot += interval } }

b.label: Open model
b.title: sends on schedule
b.html: // requests go out on schedule, whatever the server is doing fun openLoop(client: Client, ratePerSecond: Int, durationNanos: Long, histogram: LogHistogram) { val interval = 1_000_000_000L / ratePerSecond val end = System.nanoTime() + durationNanos Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { pool -> var slot = System.nanoTime() while (slot < end) { LockSupport.parkNanos(slot - System.nanoTime()) val scheduledAt = slot pool.execute { client.authorize() // later requests don't wait for this one synchronized(histogram) { histogram.record((System.nanoTime() - scheduledAt) / 1_000) } // µs from the PLANNED send } slot += interval } } }

compare.note: Both loops aim at the same rate. The closed one can't send its next request until the previous answer is back, so during a 1.4 s pause it sends nothing and records a single slow time. The open one starts each request at its planned time on a virtual thread, a very cheap kind of thread that Java 21 added, so a later request never waits for an earlier one. It times each request from its planned slot. So every request that should have gone out during the pause is counted with the wait it really had. Client stands for the program's connection to the bank, and LogHistogram is the histogram you build in this lesson's lab.

worked.title: Read the p99 of two copies from their histograms

steps.say: Two copies of the payments program report histograms with six buckets. Each bucket is labelled by the largest time it holds, in ms. Copy A handled 10,000 requests, and copy B handled 2,000.

Each copy's own p99 is the bucket where the running total reaches 99% of its count. In sorted order, copy A needs request number 9,900 (its rank): the totals go 4,000, then 9,800, then 9,950, so its p99 is in the 50 ms bucket. Copy B needs rank 1,980 and only gets there in the last bucket.
The tempting shortcut averages the two: (50 + 1,000) / 2 = 525 ms. It ignores that copy B handles only a sixth of the traffic, and the true answer can't be worked out from two percentiles anyway.
Add the counts instead, bucket by bucket, then read the p99 of the total. The rank is ceil(0.99 × 12,000) = 11,880 (ceil rounds up to a whole number), and it falls in the 100 ms bucket.
So the true p99 is between 50 and 100 ms, not 525. Notice the "between": with buckets this wide, you only know the range. Logarithmic buckets 2% apart narrow it to within 1%.
steps.code: true p99 in (50 ms, 100 ms]; the averaged figure was 5 to 10 times too high

lab.title: Build a mergeable histogram and catch a lying load test
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All 19 fail with NotImplementedError, Kotlin's way of saying a function's body is still a TODO.

In LogHistogram.kt, read bucketIndex and bucketValue. They turn a time into a bucket number and back, with buckets that grow by about 2% each. Write record, then quantile, then merge. (A quantile is a percentile written as a fraction, so the p99 is the 0.99 quantile.) The 7 tests in LogHistogramTest should pass. One uses jqwik, a library that checks a rule against many random inputs: it compares every quantile with the exact one on 30 random sets of times.

In LoadTest.kt, read PausingServer, a one-worker program on a simulated clock that can freeze, and closedLoop. Then write openLoop. Request i goes out at i * 1_000_000 / ratePerSec microseconds, whatever the server is doing, and its time is the answer time minus the send time.
Run LyingLoadTestTest. Through the 1.4 s freeze, the closed model's p99 stays under 10 ms, and yours goes over a second.
In FanOut.kt, write rootLatency: each leaf's time, with or without a hedge, and the slowest of them, because the screen waits for all. Run all the tests until they pass.
hints: quantile: return 0 if count == 0L. Otherwise val rank = maxOf(1L, ceil(q * count).toLong()). Add up counts[i] from i = 0, and at the first i where the total reaches rank, return minOf(bucketValue(i), max).

openLoop: loop over a Long i and compute val sendAt = i * 1_000_000L / ratePerSec; stop when sendAt >= durationMicros. With an Int i, i * 1_000_000 grows past the largest Int after about 2,147 requests and turns negative.
rootLatency: a leaf is hedged only when hedgeAfter != null && c.first > hedgeAfter, and its time is then minOf(c.first, hedgeAfter + c.second).

drill.title: The tail's sums, from memory
drill.prompt: Without notes: (1) A leaf is slow 1% of the time. What share of requests is slow at a fan-out of 10, 100 and 1,000? (2) How rarely may each leaf be slow, if only 1% of requests at a fan-out of 100 may be slow? (3) Write the mean response time of one worker at utilization ρ (the Greek letter rho), and its value at 90% busy for 10 ms of work. (4) Write Little's law, and use it for 400 requests a second at 120 ms each.

answer.html:
(1) P(slow) = 1 - 0.99^N
    N = 10:     1 - 0.904   = about 10%
    N = 100:    1 - 0.366   = about 63%
    N = 1,000:  1 - 0.00004 = almost 100%
(2) 1 - (1 - p)^100 = 0.01  ->  (1 - p)^100 = 0.99  ->  p = about 0.0001
    each leaf may be slow 0.01% of the time: its p99.99 has to meet the page's p99 target
(3) W = S / (1 - ρ)
    10 ms / (1 - 0.9) = 100 ms
(4) L = λ × W
    400 per second × 0.12 s = 48 requests in flight

recap: A request's response time is the work on it (service time) plus the waiting (latency): travel, and queueing in lines you can't see. Measure it from the side that waits.

Waiting grows like 1 / (1 − utilization): 10 ms of work takes 100 ms on average at 90% busy. Little's law, L = λ × W, says how many requests are in progress, which sizes things like a set of connections.
Report percentiles, not the mean. Never average the percentiles of several copies; add their histograms and read the percentile from the total.

A load test that waits for each answer stops sending when the program stalls, and hides the stall (coordinated omission). Send on a fixed schedule, and time each request from when it should have left.

Fan-out turns a rare slow answer into the normal case (1 − 0.99^100 = 63%). Hedged requests buy it back for a few percent more requests, if replicas slow down separately and the request is safe to run twice.

An SLO is a target for a measurement over a window, and what it allows to fail is the error budget. The limit: a target says how often the program may fail, but nothing about why parts fail or how to survive them.

explain.prompt: A friend shows you a load-test report that says p99 = 8 ms, and says the payments program is ready for the holiday rush. Explain what you would check before believing it.
explain.answer: First, how was the load made? If the tester keeps a fixed set of connections that each wait for an answer before sending the next request, it stops sending whenever the program stalls. Then a long pause shows up as a few slow times, and the p99 stays low. I'd want a tester that sends at a fixed rate and times each request from when it should have left. I'd also look at the maximum next to the p99: a maximum of a second with a p99 of 8 ms gives it away. Second, how busy was the program? The rush will push it much harder, and waiting grows like 1 / (1 − utilization), so a p99 measured at 50% busy says little about 90%. Third, where was it measured, and how were the copies combined? It should be measured from the side that waits, with the copies' histograms added up, never by averaging each copy's p99. Last, what does a screen do with it? If one screen needs many requests, its p99 is far worse than each request's.

deeper.html:
The p99 is a warning light more than a speedometer. Marc Brooker, an engineer at Amazon, points out that high percentiles are mostly made of waiting in line, so they rise with load whatever the code does. That makes them a poor way to tell whether a change made the code faster, and a good early sign that a system is close to overload. To judge the code's own speed, he suggests the mean, or the service time itself. Use both, for different questions.

The model behind the first rule. The rule in the first section comes from queueing theory, the mathematics of waiting lines. Its model of one worker with random arrivals and random work is called M/M/1. The two M's say that the gaps between arrivals and the amounts of work are both random in the "memoryless" way, and the 1 says there's one worker. In that model, the average number of requests in the system is ρ / (1 − ρ): 1 at 50% busy and 99 at 99% busy. Little's law turns that into the response time S / (1 − ρ).

Don't beat the promise by too much. Google's Chubby, a lock service that other programs ask before they touch something shared, was so reliable that other teams quietly assumed it never failed. So its owners took it down on purpose in any quarter of the year where it had beaten its target, to flush out the programs that would break.

Targets with a shape. A speed target often names more than one percentile, to pin down the shape of the curve: 99% of payments under 300 ms and 99.9% under 1 s. Google's SRE book also suggests separate targets for different kinds of work, such as quick requests and big bulk jobs.

Tools that collect measurements. Prometheus is a popular free program that collects numbers from running programs, and it offers two ways to measure times. A summary works out percentiles inside each program, and the Prometheus docs warn that averaging them gives statistically nonsensical values. A histogram adds up correctly across copies, but its classic buckets are few and fixed, so a percentile is only as precise as its bucket. In the docs' own example, the true p95 is about 220 ms and the estimate is 295 ms. Prometheus's newer native histograms use buckets that grow by a fixed factor, like the lab's, and its docs now recommend them over both.

Better sketches. The lab's histogram is the core of DDSketch (Masson, Rim and Lee, VLDB 2019). Its buckets guarantee a relative error, so a p99.9 of 1.8 s is reported within 1% of 1.8 s, and two sketches merge by adding counts. Sketches such as t-digest guarantee an error in the rank instead, which on very uneven timing data can still mean a large error in the reported time. HdrHistogram fixes precision in significant digits: three digits from 1 µs to an hour take about 185 KB, and recording a value takes the same short time however many it holds. It can also correct coordinated omission after the fact: recordValueWithExpectedInterval fills in the samples a stalled closed loop never took.

Load-testing settings. The guide to k6, a free load-testing tool, tests a page that takes 6 seconds to answer, for one minute. The closed model with one pretend user finishes about 10 requests. The open model, at one a second, starts 60, and needs up to 11 pretend users at once. In k6, the open model is the constant-arrival-rate (or ramping-arrival-rate) scenario. wrk2 warns that runs shorter than 10 to 20 seconds give unreliable results.

Hedging in practice. gRPC, a popular library that programs use to call each other over the network, supports hedging for each kind of request in its service config (hedgingPolicy, at most 5 attempts). Its guide warns that hedged requests must be idempotent.

Tied requests in numbers. In "The Tail at Scale", BigTable reads with a tied request sent after 1 ms on a mostly idle cluster went from a p50 of 19 ms to 16 ms, and from a p99.9 of 98 ms to 61 ms. With a large sorting job running on the same machines, the p99 fell from 108 ms to 67 ms, and the extra disk work stayed under 1%. The paper's other tricks include taking slow machines out of service while still sending them test requests, and sending a risky request to one or two leaves first. The next lesson, Faults, failures and the people who run systems, meets slow, half-broken machines again.

The framing of response time, service time and percentiles follows Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 2. Coordinated omission is not in that chapter; the wrk2 and k6 docs cover it.
